# Quip Network node

Quip Network solochain node (`quip-network-node`).

## Chain specs

Omit `--chain` to join the live public Quip Testnet (EIP-155 `20033`).
`--chain=local` is a disposable Alice-and-Bob chain. It is not the public testnet.

| Flag | Preset | Network | EIP-155 |
|------|--------|---------|--------:|
| (omit `--chain`) | `quip-testnet` | live public testnet | 20033 |
| `--chain=quip-testnet` | `quip-testnet` | live public testnet | 20033 |
| `--dev` or `--chain=dev` | Development | Alice-only local | 1337 |
| `--chain=local` | Local Testnet | Alice and Bob local | 1337 |
| `--chain=local3` | Local Testnet (3 Validators) | Alice, Bob, and Charlie local | 1337 |

Aliases for the public testnet: `quip_testnet`, `testnet`. A path argument loads that JSON file and uses the chain ID in its genesis.

Runtime 117 is the H2/H4 chain-wipe relaunch. It starts from fresh genesis and
is not an in-place upgrade of the earlier H1/H3 network. Operators must use a
fresh chain database, re-insert the H4 BABE and H2 GRANDPA keys, and sync from
the new genesis; old signed extrinsics are incompatible (`transaction_version`
is 7).

## Getting Started

Depending on your operating system and Rust version, there might be additional
packages required to compile this template. Check the
[Install](https://docs.substrate.io/install/) instructions for your platform for
the most common dependencies. Alternatively, you can use one of the [alternative
installation](#alternatives-installations) options.

Fetch solochain template code:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/paritytech/polkadot-sdk-solochain-template.git solochain-template

cd solochain-template
```

### Build

🔨 Use the following command to build the node without launching it:

```sh
cargo build --release
```

### Join the live public testnet

Omit `--chain` to select `quip-testnet` (EIP-155 `20033`).

```sh
# Live public testnet (EIP-155 20033). Default if you omit --chain.
./target/release/quip-network-node
```

### Embedded Docs

After you build the project, you can use the following command to explore its
parameters and subcommands:

```sh
./target/release/solochain-template-node -h
```

You can generate and view the [Rust
Docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-doc.html) for this template
with this command:

```sh
cargo +nightly doc --open
```

### Single-Node Development Chain

The following command starts a single-node development chain that does not
persist state. `--dev` is the Alice-only local preset (EIP-155 `1337`), not
the public testnet.

```sh
# Alice-only local chain (EIP-155 1337)
./target/release/solochain-template-node --dev
```

To purge the development chain's state, run the following command:

```sh
# Alice-only local chain (EIP-155 1337)
./target/release/solochain-template-node purge-chain --dev
```

To start the development chain with detailed logging, run the following command:

```sh
# Alice-only local chain (EIP-155 1337)
RUST_BACKTRACE=1 ./target/release/solochain-template-node -ldebug --dev
```

Development chains (`--dev` / `--chain=dev`):

- Maintain state in a `tmp` folder while the node is running.
- Use the **Alice** account as the sole validator authority.
- Use the **Alice** account as the default `sudo` account.
- Are preconfigured with a genesis state (`/node/src/chain_spec.rs`) that
  includes several pre-funded development accounts.
- Use EIP-155 chain ID `1337`.


To persist chain state between runs, specify a base path by running a command
similar to the following:

```sh
// Create a folder to use as the db base path
$ mkdir my-chain-state

// Alice-only local chain (EIP-155 1337)
$ ./target/release/solochain-template-node --dev --base-path ./my-chain-state/

// Check the folder structure created inside the base path after running the chain
$ ls ./my-chain-state
chains
$ ls ./my-chain-state/chains/
dev
$ ls ./my-chain-state/chains/dev
db keystore network
```

### Connect with Polkadot-JS Apps Front-End

After you start the node template locally, you can interact with it using the
hosted version of the [Polkadot/Substrate
Portal](https://polkadot.js.org/apps/#/explorer?rpc=ws://localhost:9944)
front-end by connecting to the local node endpoint. A hosted version is also
available on [IPFS](https://dotapps.io/). You can
also find the source code and instructions for hosting your own instance in the
[`polkadot-js/apps`](https://github.com/polkadot-js/apps) repository.

Quip uses hybrid BABE and GRANDPA consensus keys. Polkadot.js Apps does not
require custom types for Quip anymore.

### Multi-Node Local Testnet

A scripted three-validator local network is available two ways.
Both use `--chain=local3` (EIP-155 `1337`). This is not the public testnet.

- **Native build:** `scripts/start-local3.sh` builds the debug binary and starts
  three validators (Alice/Bob/Charlie) against the embedded `local3` chain spec.
- **Docker:** `docker compose up --build` starts the same three-validator
  topology in containers. See the [Docker](#docker) section below.

Both paths use the same hardcoded libp2p node-keys and bootnode peer ID, so
they're interchangeable for development.

For background on multi-node consensus, see [Simulate a
network](https://docs.substrate.io/tutorials/build-a-blockchain/simulate-network/).

## Template Structure

A Substrate project such as this consists of a number of components that are
spread across a few directories.

### Node

A blockchain node is an application that allows users to participate in a
blockchain network. Substrate-based blockchain nodes expose a number of
capabilities:

- Networking: Substrate nodes use the [`libp2p`](https://libp2p.io/) networking
  stack to allow the nodes in the network to communicate with one another.
- Consensus: Blockchains must have a way to come to
  [consensus](https://docs.substrate.io/fundamentals/consensus/) on the state of
  the network. Substrate makes it possible to supply custom consensus engines
  and also ships with several consensus mechanisms that have been built on top
  of [Web3 Foundation
  research](https://research.web3.foundation/Polkadot/protocols/NPoS).
- RPC Server: A remote procedure call (RPC) server is used to interact with
  Substrate nodes.

There are several files in the `node` directory. Take special note of the
following:

- [`chain_spec.rs`](./node/src/chain_spec.rs): A [chain
  specification](https://docs.substrate.io/build/chain-spec/) is a source code
  file that defines a Substrate chain's initial (genesis) state. Chain
  specifications are useful for development and testing, and critical when
  architecting the launch of a production chain. Take note of the
  `development_config` and `testnet_genesis` functions. These functions are
  used to define the genesis state for the local development chain
  configuration. These functions identify some [well-known
  accounts](https://docs.substrate.io/reference/command-line-tools/subkey/) and
  use them to configure the blockchain's initial state.
- [`service.rs`](./node/src/service.rs): This file defines the node
  implementation. Take note of the libraries that this file imports and the
  names of the functions it invokes. In particular, there are references to
  consensus-related topics, such as the [block finalization and
  forks](https://docs.substrate.io/fundamentals/consensus/#finalization-and-forks)
  and other [consensus
  mechanisms](https://docs.substrate.io/fundamentals/consensus/#default-consensus-models)
  such as BABE for block authoring and GRANDPA for finality.


### Runtime

In Substrate, the terms "runtime" and "state transition function" are analogous.
Both terms refer to the core logic of the blockchain that is responsible for
validating blocks and executing the state changes they define. The Substrate
project in this repository uses
[FRAME](https://docs.substrate.io/learn/runtime-development/#frame) to construct
a blockchain runtime. FRAME allows runtime developers to declare domain-specific
logic in modules called "pallets". At the heart of FRAME is a helpful [macro
language](https://docs.substrate.io/reference/frame-macros/) that makes it easy
to create pallets and flexibly compose them to create blockchains that can
address [a variety of needs](https://substrate.io/ecosystem/projects/).

Review the [FRAME runtime implementation](./runtime/src/lib.rs) included in this
template and note the following:

- This file configures several pallets to include in the runtime. Each pallet
  configuration is defined by a code block that begins with `impl
  $PALLET_NAME::Config for Runtime`.
- The pallets are composed into a single runtime by way of the
  [#[runtime]](https://paritytech.github.io/polkadot-sdk/master/frame_support/attr.runtime.html)
  macro, which is part of the [core FRAME pallet
  library](https://docs.substrate.io/reference/frame-pallets/#system-pallets).

### Custody vesting

Both runtimes include stock vesting at pallet index 32. Mainnet allocation
amounts, custody identity, recipients and tranche terms remain unresolved and
block mainnet export. Genesis creates no vesting schedules; later signed
multisig custody transfers issue one schedule per tranche.

Vesting constrains the recipient's **total balance**, including held stake:
ordinary transfers preserve `total >= frozen`. Held stake discounts the amount
that must stay free, so a pre-bonded account with enough held stake can transfer
a new grant immediately, even before its vesting start. Both initial `bond`
and `bond_extra` from vested funds are intentionally allowed. Guaranteeing that
the grant itself stays illiquid requires a new owner decision and a hold-based
design; the current pallet does not provide that guarantee.

The minimum vested transfer is `100 * EXISTENTIAL_DEPOSIT` (0.1 QUIP). This raises
the cost of filling an account's 28 schedule slots: at the former ED floor,
28 × ED (0.028 QUIP) could fill them, while council Root force-remove is denied.
The higher floor prices this attack; it does not prevent it. Completed schedules
can be cleaned up with `vest`/`vest_other`; merging requires the recipient.

The immutable pre-vesting evidence is in
[`tests/fixtures/pre-vesting/manifest.json`](tests/fixtures/pre-vesting/manifest.json).
The original `f7da5ec` post-vesting capture is preserved in
[`tests/fixtures/post-vesting-f7da5ec/manifest.json`](tests/fixtures/post-vesting-f7da5ec/manifest.json);
its validation claims predate the review corrections above. The corrected
100×ED capture is recorded separately in
[`tests/fixtures/post-vesting-fix/manifest.json`](tests/fixtures/post-vesting-fix/manifest.json).
SDK weights remain provisional until the reference-machine run and final
metadata/storage/signing review tracked by
[QUI-2101](https://linear.app/quip-network/issue/QUI-2101/vesting-release-gate-reference-machine-weights-and-metadata-re),
owned by `roman@postquant.xyz`.

### Pallets

The runtime in this project is constructed using many FRAME pallets that ship
with [the Substrate
repository](https://github.com/paritytech/polkadot-sdk/tree/master/substrate/frame) and a
template pallet that is [defined in the
`pallets`](./pallets/template/src/lib.rs) directory.

A FRAME pallet is comprised of a number of blockchain primitives, including:

- Storage: FRAME defines a rich set of powerful [storage
  abstractions](https://docs.substrate.io/build/runtime-storage/) that makes it
  easy to use Substrate's efficient key-value database to manage the evolving
  state of a blockchain.
- Dispatchables: FRAME pallets define special types of functions that can be
  invoked (dispatched) from outside of the runtime in order to update its state.
- Events: Substrate uses
  [events](https://docs.substrate.io/build/events-and-errors/) to notify users
  of significant state changes.
- Errors: When a dispatchable fails, it returns an error.

These functions identify some well-known accounts and use them to configure the blockchain's initial state.

Review the FRAME runtime implementation included in this template and note the following:

  • This file configures several pallets to include in the runtime. Each pallet configuration is defined by a code block that begins with impl $PALLET_NAME::Config for Runtime.
  • The pallets are composed into a single runtime by way of the #[runtime] macro, which is part of the core FRAME pallet library.

Alternatives Installations

Instead of installing dependencies and building this source directly, consider the following alternatives.

Nix

Install nix and nix-direnv for a fully plug-and-play experience for setting up the development environment. To get all the correct dependencies, activate direnv direnv allow.

Docker

A multi-stage Dockerfile builds the quip-network-node binary on top of debian:bookworm-slim (~80 MB runtime image). The image exposes the binary directly as ENTRYPOINT, so any Substrate CLI flag works at docker run time.

Build

docker build -t quip-network-node:local .

The first build compiles the full workspace and takes a while. BuildKit cache mounts (declared in the Dockerfile) keep the cargo registry and target directory between local rebuilds.

Pre-built images

Every push to main and every git tag publishes an image to the project's GitLab Container Registry, so you don't have to build locally:

docker pull registry.gitlab.com/quip.network/quip-validator/quip-network-node:latest

Tag scheme:

  • :latest — tip of main. Floating, advances on every merge.
  • :sha-<short> — pinned to a specific commit on main or to a tagged release.
  • :<git-tag> — pinned to a release tag (e.g. :v0.1.0).

Run as a validator

# Three-validator local chain (EIP-155 1337). Not the public testnet.
docker run --rm -v quip-data:/data -p 9944:9944 -p 30333:30333 \
  quip-network-node:local \
  --chain=local3 --base-path=/data \
  --validator --alice \
  --unsafe-rpc-external --rpc-cors=all

--unsafe-rpc-external is required because Substrate refuses to combine --rpc-external with --validator by default (a safety guard against exposing a validator's RPC to the public internet). For local development the unsafe flag is fine; for production validators you almost certainly do not want any external RPC at all.

Run as a full node

Same command, omit --validator (and the --alice/--bob/--charlie shortcut):

# Three-validator local chain (EIP-155 1337). Not the public testnet.
docker run --rm -v quip-data:/data -p 9944:9944 -p 30333:30333 \
  quip-network-node:local \
  --chain=local3 --base-path=/data \
  --bootnodes=/dns/<bootnode-host>/tcp/30333/p2p/<peer-id> \
  --rpc-external --rpc-cors=all

Local 3-node network via docker-compose

docker-compose.yml reproduces scripts/start-local3.sh in containers. Each service passes --chain=local3 (EIP-155 1337). This is not the public testnet.

docker compose up --build           # start local3 (EIP-155 1337)
docker compose down                 # stop, keep chain state
docker compose down -v              # stop and wipe state

Then connect Polkadot.js Apps to ws://localhost:9944 (node1), ws://localhost:9945 (node2), or ws://localhost:9946 (node3).

Public testnet

quip-testnet is the live public testnet ("AGLS" tokens, 12 decimals, EIP-155 20033). Omitting --chain, or using quip-testnet, quip_testnet or testnet, loads the exact raw artifact embedded from chain-specs/quip-testnet.json. Its historical runtime and genesis storage are independent of the runtime compiled into a new node binary.

The file is a byte-for-byte copy of the public testnet raw spec published as chain-specs/aglais-network.json in the nodes.quip.network repository. It is vendored here as quip-testnet.json because the local filename identifies the network it serves; the upstream name refers to the same network under its older AGLS label. The upstream file's SHA-256 was verified against GitLab's reported content hash at upstream commit d65ab5b7ad62dad2de603c2611c14a72b24c1537. Its pinned SHA-256 is 0aeeddaf5b546a491d96c35fd636614c6ab42d4e5d9724126182b52c8c694ad4; its genesis hash is 0x542a9915acf840b8940d35ca6de242f669a0c6e3b40f9a8d8c14b9bf7b8ebecb. The blocking live-testnet-spec CI job checks the file's exact bytes, including formatting. Node tests check all four aliases and the genesis hash.

The registered runtime quip_testnet preset remains available through GenesisBuilder for policy auditing. Exporting that preset with a newly compiled runtime does not reproduce the published live genesis. dev, local, local3 and rehearsal continue to use their runtime builders. The unfinished quip-mainnet and quip-testnet-relaunch presets have no built-in node chain aliases.

Quickstart (built node)

cargo build --release -p quip-network-node
# Live public testnet (EIP-155 20033). Omit --chain for the same artifact.
./target/release/quip-network-node --chain=quip-testnet --base-path=./quip-data

The three canonical bootnodes (bootnode-{1,2,3}.aglais.quip.network) are embedded in the raw file, with the live protocol ID agls-network and AGLS properties unchanged.

Using the raw file with an existing image

Explicit file loading also works with existing images; those images do not acquire this new embedded-artifact behavior merely because this repository changed. Validate the checked-out artifact before using its path:

python3 scripts/check-live-testnet-spec.py

docker run --rm -v "$PWD/chain-specs:/spec:ro" -v quip-data:/data \
  -p 9944:9944 -p 30333:30333 \
  registry.gitlab.com/quip.network/quip-validator/quip-network-node:v0.3.0 \
  --chain=/spec/quip-testnet.json --base-path=/data

The vendored path represents the public network currently selected by the four aliases. A future approved relaunch must replace the artifact and update its checksum, genesis-hash tests and provenance in the same reviewed activation commit. The old artifact remains in Git history and release provenance. A new genesis requires fresh databases; this change does not activate a relaunch.

CI also starts a non-validator against a temporary copy with only bootnodes removed, checks its genesis over RPC, and restarts the same genesis-only DB. Isolation relies on empty bootnodes and reserved-peer lists, disabled mDNS, and disabled ordinary peers. The pinned litep2p backend still runs periodic Kademlia queries. The smoke test therefore verifies empty bootnodes before launch, observes at least ten seconds after RPC readiness, requires a Kademlia query log marker, and rejects outbound dial logs across the full run. Missing discovery logging fails the smoke test instead of silently shortening coverage. This smoke test checks startup and DB reopen, not the shipped peer list, live sync, consensus, or compatibility with an existing production DB.

Running a validator

Operator validator slots are committed in runtime/src/genesis_config_presets.rs. The scripts/derive-operator-keys.sh helper derives operator keys.

aiSummary.oneLiner: A minimal, out-of-the-box Substrate node template for rapid blockchain prototyping in Rust.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: The Quip Protocol RS repository provides a streamlined, functional Substrate node template designed to serve as a starting point for building custom blockchains. It pre-configures essential components of the Substrate framework, allowing developers to immediately compile and run a local, single-node network without complex initial setup. The project focuses on minimizing boilerplate code, providing a clean slate for developers to integrate their own custom runtime logic, known as pallets. By offering a ready-to-run environment, it significantly accelerates the initial prototyping phase for decentralized applications and bespoke blockchain networks.
keyFeatures: Minimalist node configuration: Provides a stripped-down, essential Substrate setup that avoids unnecessary pre-installed pallets and bloat.
Out-of-the-box compilation: Ensures the node can be immediately compiled and launched as a local development network using standard Rust tooling.
Custom pallet readiness: Offers a clean, documented runtime environment specifically structured for the easy integration of custom business logic.
Standardized Substrate architecture: Adheres strictly to the established design patterns and conventions of the broader Polkadot and Substrate ecosystem.
Local development focus: Optimizes the initial configuration for rapid, single-node testing rather than immediate production deployment.

useCases.title: Rapid blockchain prototyping
useCases.description: A development team uses the template to quickly spin up a functional local network to demonstrate a new decentralized application concept.

useCases.title: Custom pallet development
useCases.description: Provide a clean, isolated environment to develop and test custom Substrate pallets before integrating them into a larger, complex network.

useCases.title: Educational experimentation
useCases.description: Allow developers to explore the Substrate framework and learn core blockchain architecture by modifying a working, minimal node.

useCases.title: Hackathon project acceleration
useCases.description: Accelerate the development of blockchain prototypes during hackathons by providing a reliable, ready-to-run node template.

aiSummary.whoIsItFor: Blockchain developers, Rust engineers, and students looking for a reliable, minimal starting point to build custom networks using the Substrate framework. Familiarity with the relevant ecosystem workflows is highly recommended for optimal usage.
